title: Modern Chinese Literature
tagline: The literary revolution, Lu Xun’s fiction, his essays and prose poems, the new poetry, the modern essay, fiction of the 1920s and 1930s, the left-wing movement, modern drama, Shen Congwen and the Beijing and Shanghai schools, and literature of the war years
summary: Modern Chinese literature began with the New Culture Movement’s call to write in the vernacular and to remake Chinese culture. This course reads the writers of the years from the literary revolution of 1917 to 1949 — Lu Xun above all, the new poets and essayists, the novelists and playwrights of the 1920s and 1930s such as Ba Jin, Mao Dun, Lao She, Cao Yu and Shen Congwen, the modernists of Shanghai and Eileen Chang, and the literature of the war years.
overview: A course on Chinese literature from 1917 to 1949: the republic of literature that was built when the written language fell off its throne.

It follows the decade-by-decade experiments of the new literature—the language revolution, the invention of the modern author, the quarrels between schools, and the way war reorganised the literary field—while reading major works closely alongside the theories of the previous course.

By the end, students should handle the modern period as a set of solved problems (form, institution, value) rather than a canon, and recognise the same problems still running beneath contemporary writing.
outcomes: Explain the language revolution as an institutional event (institutions, print capitalism, education) and not only as an idea
Read Lu Xun's fiction and prose poems with a full apparatus of narrative voice, irony and figure
Reconstruct the field of the 1920s–30s—literary societies, journals, schools, quarrels—and interpret a work through its position
Analyse the forms of new poetry (free verse, the Crescent school, the modernists) as solutions to the metrical problem inherited from classical poetry
Trace the rise of the modern essay and its styles of subjectivity
Evaluate the left-wing turn, wartime re-organisation and the Yan'an settlement as changes in the rules of the game
Argue an interpretation of a major work (Border Town, Thunderstorm, Fortress Besieged) with textual evidence
Relate categories of literary theory—genre, institution, interpretation—to concrete modern cases

chapters.title: The literary revolution
chapters.summary: Hu Shi’s and Chen Duxiu’s manifestos of 1917, *New Youth*, the May Fourth Movement and the victory of the vernacular.

chapters.title: Lu Xun’s fiction
chapters.summary: *A Madman’s Diary*, *The True Story of Ah Q* and the stories of *Call to Arms* and *Wandering*.

chapters.title: Lu Xun’s essays and prose poems
chapters.summary: The polemical essays, *Wild Grass* and *Dawn Blossoms Plucked at Dusk*.

chapters.title: The new poetry
chapters.summary: From Hu Shi’s experiments and Guo Moruo’s *The Goddesses* to the Crescent poets Xu Zhimo and Wen Yiduo, and Li Jinfa, Dai Wangshu and Ai Qing.

chapters.title: The modern essay
chapters.summary: Zhou Zuoren, Zhu Ziqing, Bing Xin, Yu Dafu and Lin Yutang, and the range of the vernacular essay.

chapters.title: Fiction of the 1920s and 1930s
chapters.summary: Yu Dafu, Mao Dun’s *Midnight*, Ba Jin’s *Family* and Lao She’s *Rickshaw Boy*.

chapters.title: The left-wing movement
chapters.summary: The League of Left-Wing Writers, the debates on revolutionary literature, and the place of politics in writing.

chapters.title: Modern drama
chapters.summary: The spoken drama from its beginnings to Cao Yu’s *Thunderstorm* and *Sunrise*, and Tian Han and Xia Yan.

chapters.title: Shen Congwen and the Beijing and Shanghai schools
chapters.summary: Shen Congwen’s *Border Town*, the Beijing school, Shanghai’s New Sensationists, and Eileen Chang.

chapters.title: Literature of the war years
chapters.summary: Writing during the war against Japan, Yan’an and the *Talks at the Yan’an Forum on Literature and Art* of 1942, Zhao Shuli, and Qian Zhongshu’s *Fortress Besieged*.

history.title: The literary revolution begins
history.detail: Hu Shi and Chen Duxiu in New Youth raise the slogan against archaic writing; the vernacular is proposed as the language of literature.

history.title: A Madman's Diary
history.detail: Lu Xun's diary fiction appears in New Youth: the vernacular arrives already carrying its hardest masterpiece.

history.title: Schools organise
history.detail: The Literary Research Society and the Creation Society are founded; journals, societies and quarrels constitute the new field.
history.people: Zheng Zhen duo, Guo Moruo and others

history.title: Mass readership enters
history.detail: Centenary enthusiasm for Dream of the Red Chamber and the rise of fiction readers make interpretation a public market.

history.title: Regional colours
history.detail: Borderland and local-colour writing redistribute literary geography away from the capital.

history.title: The Left-Wing Writers League
history.detail: The League is founded in Shanghai; class literature becomes an organised programme with its own budgets and martyrs.

history.title: Fortress Besieged serialised
history.detail: Qian Zhongshu's ironic novel of ideas begins in the weekly Frontier Trench; comedy survives inside the age of commitment.

history.title: The Yan'an Forum
history.detail: Mao's talks define literature and art for workers, peasants and soldiers; the terms of the field are rewritten by policy.
